entities.summary:
Wang Lü was a renowned Chinese painter, calligrapher, poet, and physician who played a pivotal role in the Ming dynasty (1368–1644).

Born in the early 14th century, Wang Lü's artistic prowess and intellectual curiosity made him a sought-after figure in the imperial court. He was known for his innovative techniques in landscape painting and his mastery of the traditional art of calligraphy.

Wang Lü's contributions extend beyond the realm of art, as he was also a skilled physician who developed new treatments for various ailments. His work in this field led to significant advancements in the understanding and treatment of diseases, particularly in the areas of Chinese medicine and pharmacology.

Despite his many achievements, Wang Lü's life was marked by personal struggles and controversies. His complex relationships with powerful patrons and rivals led to a series of high-stakes diplomatic maneuvers that shaped the course of Ming dynasty politics.

In the end, Wang Lü's legacy was cemented as one of the greatest artists and intellectuals of his time, with his works continuing to inspire and influence generations of Chinese artists and scholars.

This painter's most famous words, 'The world is not a picture,' encapsulate his philosophy on the fleeting nature of beauty and the importance of living in the present.

Wang Lü's remarkable life serves as a testament to the enduring power of art and creativity in shaping human understanding and experience.

entities.summary:
Wang Lü (Wang Li; style name Andao; 1332–after 1377) was a Ming-dynasty physician, landscape painter, calligrapher, and poet whose journeys through Mount Hua produced a celebrated album combining images and travel prose. A literati polymath, he treated painting as investigation—recording peaks, paths, and bodily experience of terrain.

His Hua Mountain album is a landmark of early Ming topographical landscape, bridging medical attentiveness to the body with pictorial observation. Though death date is uncertain, his surviving work shaped later travel-painting ideals.

Wang Lü exemplifies Ming scholar-artists who made landscape a form of empirical knowledge.
